title: The last two of al-Baqarah
hookLine: our Lord, do not burden us beyond what we can bear (2:285–286)

lines: A VERSE THAT FELT TOO HEAVY.
ON THEIR KNEES: MORE THAN WE CAN BEAR.
cards: Have you ever read a rule and felt your stomach drop? Not because you wanted to break it, but because you knew you couldn't keep it.

That happened to the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ near the end of Surah al-Baqarah. A verse came saying that whether you show what's in yourselves or hide it, Allah will bring you to account for it.
What's in yourselves: the thoughts you never chose. Sahih Muslim records that they came to the Prophet and fell to their knees: this is more than we can bear.
What happened next became the surah's ending, two verses still said at night.

teach.b: The Prophet told them not to turn away but to say: we hear and we obey; Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the return. They said it, and the words came back to them as scripture.

Verse two eighty-five describes the messenger and the believers who believe in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, and who say exactly that. Then verse two eighty-six opens with the answer to their fear.
Pickthall: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.
Scope, in Arabic wus', means capacity, width, room. You are asked for what you have room for. Each soul gets what it earned, and bears what it did.
Then the verse becomes a list of pleas, the ones the companions made on their knees.

teach.h: DON'T TAKE US TO TASK IF WE FORGET.
teach.b: Our Lord, don't take us to task if we forget or make mistakes. Don't lay on us a burden like the ones laid on those before us. Don't load us with what we have no strength for.
Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. You are our Protector.
The report in Sahih Muslim adds that after each plea, Allah answered: I have done so.
The worry about unchosen thoughts is answered too: other hadith say a person isn't held to account for passing thoughts they don't act on or speak.
And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him. A heavy verse, then a gentle ending.

how: Muslims recite the last two verses of Surah al-Baqarah (2:285–286) at night before sleep, following the hadith that they suffice whoever recites them; the pleas of 2:286 are also said as a du'a on their own.

o: a reward stored up for the next life
a burden laid on earlier peoples
capacity: the room each soul is given

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: they will be enough for him

s: the companions accepted the heavy verse without a word
they came to the Prophet on their knees: more than we can bear.
2:286 says no soul is tasked beyond its scope
wus': capacity, the room you've been given.
the last two verses are recited only in Ramadan
Bukhari: whoever recites them at night, they suffice him.

games.q: a verse feels impossible to keep. you and the others go to the Prophet. what does he tell you to say?
o: we cannot bear it, so we'll wait
we hear and we obey; Your forgiveness, our Lord
games.why: they said it, and 2:285–286 came down with their words, and the promise: no soul beyond its scope (Sahih Muslim).

practice: Let the pleas of verse two eighty-six pass by, one per breath: with one real slip in mind, don't take us to task if we forget or make mistakes; with one worry, don't load us with what we have no strength for; then pardon, forgiveness, mercy.
Rest on the line beneath them all: not beyond its scope. If you pray, you can recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah tonight, or just their pleas.

wordCard.voice: Wus', capacity: the scope Allah tasks no soul beyond, in the last two verses of al-Baqarah, two eighty-five and six.

orig.s: لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
orig.note: Arabic: Allah tasks no soul except within its capacity (2:286).

carryVoice: Your line: not beyond what we bear. It answered people on their knees. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.
